# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the middle one is in Keel's voice (*you send them*, *Contacts page*) rather than mine like the other two.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study, and my pick of people I know by name stands as I made it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a Keel search (I pick a list; Keel makes a link for each, and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are, like a hearing-loss group; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated, but the number beside it is 'median 4 days out of 7', which sits inside my 4-to-7 range and so seems to argue against the verdict; the number that actually decides it, 4 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, is only in the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows its count, n and bar, but the Frequency card says the split three times in different shapes, Importance repeats '7 of 7 put it in their two', and the count line is printed twice, so it takes a second pass to see that the split is one person short.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are word for word the beliefs I checked, and Prevalence and Frequency are mine in my study's words (window, actor, 4 to 7 days).
screens.why_b4: The page never says what a frequency split means for AirCaps (for example, that many lose the thread 2 to 3 days a week rather than daily, or whether that changes the wedge or the pitch); 'What it measures' only explains the rule.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible everywhere, but three beliefs are called 'Holding up' and the 7-of-7 results stand bare, with no word that seven people is a small sample to read 'at least 8 in 10 of US deaf adults' from.
screens.instead: People disagree on how often: 4 of 7 lose the thread on 4 or more days a week, one short of your bar of 5; the other 3 do 2 to 3 days. The pain is real and ranked first by all 7, but expect many buyers to need the glasses for some meals and meetings, not every day. 7 people is a small sample.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Holding up* sits right on top of *7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7*, so I see that it held and the count that decides it in one line.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells all for me, a marker at 6 labelled *at least 8 in 10*, and an axis of 0 to 7 show what is counted, over how many people, and where my bar sits, though the strip itself never says *said yes*.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence and *At least 8 in 10 ... lost track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people in the last 7 days* are my band and my event, not stretched to *nearly all*.
screens.why_b4: *Common among these 7* tells me the problem shows up for my wedge, and it sends me to Frequency and Importance, which matters because the stage page already flagged Frequency as disputed.
screens.why_b5: n is on the screen (*7 answered · 7 counted*), the small group is named (*a lean, not a call*), and the So line keeps the claim to *these 7*.
screens.instead: Drop *— the most recent time it happened* from the Asked line; it belongs to the story after a Yes and makes the gate read like a different question.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, People disagree, sits right beside its deciding numbers: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4 days, against a bar of 5 of 7, so 1 short, with a median of 4 days.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows one cell per person over 7 counted, 4 for and 3 against, with the marker at 5, and the chart's ticks and median read at a glance; the only oddity is a 0 tick on a scale no one could answer 0 on.
screens.why_b3: Frequency is named, and the belief line uses my question's own clause, 'lose track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people on 4 to 7 days out of 7', which is what I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me onward but doesn't say what a near-miss means for my wedge, for example that many in my segment hit this 2 to 3 days a week rather than most days.
screens.why_b5: The small n is said plainly ('a lean, not a call'), but the Asked line tacks on 'the most recent time it happened', which misdescribes a count-of-days question and makes me wonder what people actually answered.
screens.instead: Drop 'the most recent time it happened' from the Asked line, and have the So line say: 3 of 7 hit this on fewer than 4 days, so my most-days picture may be too strong; check whether the weekly-but-not-daily group still ranks it in their top two on the Importance card.

screens.why_b1: The card says Holding up with 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together at the top.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 7 people each picked two and the bars count 14 picks, my row is marked as the problem I named with 7 for, and the strip shows 7 cells with the marker at 5, so it reads at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked, five things and following fast or noisy talk included.
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly says top two rather than first, but it never tells me what this means for AirCaps; it could say this is settled and that Frequency, which split 4 to 3, is what to dig into next.
screens.why_b5: n is on the screen, the small group is called a lean and not a call, and the So line stops itself from claiming the problem ranks first.
screens.instead: All 7 put following fast or noisy talk in their two, a lean among 7; importance isn't your risk, Frequency is, so go find out how many days a week it actually bites.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see that it held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the 7 people's last conversations rung by rung, each rung marked for or against, with my line drawn under 'Missed a little, caught up quickly' and the strip's marker at 5; all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief line and the bar rung 'Missed a little, caught up quickly' are the ones I checked, word for word.
screens.why_b4: The So line names the gap (3 caught only the gist, 3 nodded along), but 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is a stock line and doesn't say what it means for the glasses.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so it doesn't oversell 6 of 7.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of 7: half get only the gist and half nod along. The glasses have to get people past the gist in group talk, so test that on the solution study.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on Holding up with 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together.
screens.why_b3: The line is named Current solution and the belief is word for word the one I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what this means for AirCaps; the footer lines only explain why Frequency and Prevalence have no box, and Importance's clean 7 of 7 goes unmentioned.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay honest (1 against, 1 asked, the 6 of 7 visible), but the screen is headed 'When a line fails' over a line that held, which made me first read it as a failure.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's answer is new to me: someone deaf on one side gets by with seating (end seat, good side toward the group), so single-sided loss may be a weaker part of my wedge than the bilateral users I wrote for.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 7. The one who gets by is deaf on one side and manages with where they sit, so aim the first pairs at people with loss in both ears, and note that Importance held 7 of 7 with nobody against.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check that I actually talk with hearing people regularly before asking about those conversations.
screens.why2: Short and plain; 'hearing people' is exactly how I and other deaf people talk about them.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people every week, since that is my daily life at work, in shops and with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate question, and the gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It matches the segment of talking with hearing people every week, and nothing about any product or the founder's terms comes through.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to say, but 'I'll read 2 options' says the digit and is clunky for a yes-or-no; §17 says to end the screener with just 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you talk with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether one of those conversations went wrong for me lately.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is exactly how I'd put it when the talk moves too fast or the room is too loud and I miss where it went.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me this past week, at the shop counter, at work or at dinner with hearing friends.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and the chips beside it belong to the story box after a Yes, so they don't muddy the gate.
screens.why5: It asks about my problem in plain terms and nothing about a product, captions or the company's idea reaches me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, then "Yes or no", easy to take in once even read by a captioned or spoken AI.
screens.why7: The gate names the window and the costly moment (losing track), not the circumstance every member is in, so someone who followed fine can truly say No and the share can go either way, with no escape as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, I lost track of a conversation this week, so asking how many days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Lose track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people' is how I'd say it myself; I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I missed what people were saying at work, at the shop or at dinner, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer, none overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the one way out.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'conversation is too fast or too noisy to follow' as losing track, in my words, and nothing about a product or 'deaf and hard-of-hearing adults' as a label reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question, then 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall', which I can hold after hearing it once.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the 7-day window, from 1 to 7 in order, with no 0 and no bands, and the one 'I can't recall' escape sits apart, so the founder's low can split the buttons for and against.

screens.why1: Right after saying how many days I lost track, asking which part of talking with hearing people I'd most like easier follows naturally.
screens.why2: Most rows are how I'd say it, but 'not being worn out by listening' reads backwards after 'made easier', and I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I live every one of these every week, so I can pick without guessing.
screens.why4: Announcements in shops and stations and phone and video calls are not face-to-face conversations at all, and 'getting a word in' is the joining half that 'following fast or noisy talk' leaves out, so the rows don't all sit on the same ground.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but the own row has shrunk to 'following' and dropped 'joining', and it mostly repeats the 'too fast or too noisy' moment instead of naming the task.
screens.why6: Five short rows read as a list I could hold, with one escape said last, though the 'not being worn out' row sounds odd heard.
screens.why7: The own item is there with None of these at the first ask, but two rivals drift to another channel or setting (phone and video calls, announcements), which the card names as a pitfall, and one row is a bad outcome rather than a task.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of talking with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Following talk that's fast or noisy · Getting a word in at the right moment · Catching who is speaking in a group · Keeping up when people turn away or cover their mouths · Staying sharp to the end of a long conversation · None of these

screens.why1: Right after I picked what I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how my last go at following a conversation actually went.
screens.why2: "How did following a conversation with hearing people in noise go?" is clumsy, and I'd say "in a noisy place" rather than "in noise", so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: My last conversation might have been signing with a deaf friend or a quiet chat at home, so I'd have to guess which conversation it means: the last one, or the last noisy one with hearing people.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from following nearly everything to not following at all, "mostly nodded along" is exactly what I do, and "I can't recall" fits because nobody else can follow a conversation for me.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but the situation shrank from "too fast or too noisy" to "in noise" alone, so a fast-talking table in a quiet room drops out.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list of five, but the stem says "conversation" twice in one breath and makes me work out which conversation is meant.
screens.why7: Every rung is on one measure, how much of the conversation I followed; the first two are today's way working and the last three fall short, ending in not following at all; and the one escape is the right one for an act that can't be handed off.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you talked face to face with hearing people somewhere noisy or fast. How much of the conversation did you follow? Followed nearly everything said; missed a little, caught up quickly; caught the gist, missed the details; lost the thread and mostly nodded along; could not follow it at all; or I can't recall.
